newsitem.title: USA: Alabama seeks image boost from Mercedes plant.
newsitem.headline: Alabama seeks image boost from Mercedes plant.

text.p: The opening of a new Mercedez-Benz AG sport utility plant in Alabama this week is viewed as a chance for renewal in Alabama, a proud state trying to ovecome perceptions created by a dark past.
Alabama shocked the auto industry in 1993 by offering more than $250 million in state, local and private incentives to land the $300 million plant in Vance, Ala., near Tuscaloosa.

Officials said Wednesday they pursued the project so aggressively because they wanted the state to capture some of the luster of Mercedes' three-pointed star and its reputation as a world-class automaker.

The plant is symbolic of Alabama's "arrival" as a modern economic power that is finally ready to shed the guilt of its past associations with slavery and racism, said Culpepper Clark, dean of the University of Alabama's College of Communication.
"Alabama may be the most Southern place on Earth," Clark said. "We are the cradle of the Confederacy and the cradle of the civil rights movement."

The German luxury car maker's first U.S. plant will employ up to 1,500 people by early 1998. It will build about 65,000 M-Class compact sport utility vehicles annually, with about half of the luxury trucks, to be priced in the mid-$30,000 range, earmarked for export.

Government and business leaders justified their investment Wednesday by saying they believe the plant can attract the attention of businesses that once viewed Alabama as a backwater that tried to quash the civil rights movement in the 1950s and '60s.
"We have found that Mercedes-Benz is a magnet," said Elmer Harris, chief executive officer of Alabama Power Co. "It has the chance to change the world's perception about us."

He credits the Mercedes' decision with catching the eye of three large steel companies, LTV Corp.. Sumitomo Corp. and British Steel Plc, which eventually built a new mini-mill joint venture, Trico Steel, in Decatur, Ala.

So far, Mercedes investment has led to nine automotive suppliers moving to Alabama with the promise of 1,500 more jobs. State and local officials argue that their investment forms the backbone of a new automotive industry that could attract even more jobs to the state.
More than 60,000 Alabamans have applied for 1,000 jobs at the plant, which offers starting wages of $13.25 an hour, rising to $18.10 after 24 months.
Alabama joins a host of other southern U.S. states that have attracted foreign automakers in recent years.
Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG opened a plant near Spartanburg, S.C., last year and Volkswagen AG's Audi AG luxury car unit is exploring production sites in the South.
Toyota Motor Corp. has located in Kentucky, while Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. chose Tennessee.
